title: PACELC
description: Go beyond CAP with the PACELC framework: when partitioned choose availability or consistency, else choose latency or consistency, with real database classifications.

segments.text: CAP theorem says during a network partition, you choose availability or consistency. But here's the thing: partitions are rare. Most of the time your network is fine. So what trade-off are you actually making day to day? Daniel Abadi proposed PACELC to answer exactly that question, and it's far more useful for real architecture decisions.

PACELC reads as: if Partition, choose Availability or Consistency. Else, choose Latency or Consistency. The 'else' clause is the key insight. When the network is healthy, every replication strategy still trades latency for consistency. Synchronous replication gives consistency but adds latency. Asynchronous gives low latency but risks stale reads.

DynamoDB is PA/EL. During a partition, it chooses availability: your writes succeed even if some replicas are unreachable. When there's no partition, it chooses low latency: single-digit millisecond reads and writes using eventual consistency by default. You can opt into strongly consistent reads, but they cost twice as much and have higher latency.

Google Spanner is PC/EC. It always chooses consistency. During a partition, writes block until the partition heals. When there's no partition, it still pays for consistency with TrueTime-based synchronous replication across continents. A write in Spanner takes roughly seven milliseconds even between nearby regions. That's the consistency tax you pay on every single write.
segments.thought_prompt: Which businesses can afford 7ms write latency for global consistency? Which cannot?

segments.text: Cassandra is PA/EL by default, but it's actually configurable per query. With consistency level ONE, you get PA/EL: fast, available, eventually consistent. With consistency level ALL, you get PC/EC: every replica must respond. QUORUM gives you a middle ground. This per-query tuning is Cassandra's superpower and its biggest source of misconfiguration bugs.

MongoDB is PA/EC, an unusual combination. During a partition, secondaries can serve reads, choosing availability. But when the network is healthy, it chooses consistency over latency: all reads go to the primary by default, and write concern majority ensures durability. This means MongoDB accepts higher normal-case latency to guarantee consistent reads.

Let's see them side by side. PA/EL systems like DynamoDB and Cassandra prioritize speed and uptime at the cost of sometimes showing stale data. PC/EC systems like Spanner prioritize correctness at the cost of latency and availability. PA/EC systems like MongoDB try to be available during failures but consistent during normal operation. Each reflects a different business requirement.

How do you choose? Ask two questions. First: during a network partition, can your users tolerate errors, or must they see data even if it's stale? That's your PA versus PC decision. Second: during normal operation, do your users care more about speed or accuracy? That's your EL versus EC decision. The answers are different for a social media feed versus a banking ledger.
segments.thought_prompt: For a ride-sharing app showing driver locations, which PACELC category would you choose and why?

segments.text: Real systems often mix PACELC categories within the same application. Your user profile might be PA/EL because showing a slightly stale bio is fine. Your payment processing must be PC/EC because double-charging is catastrophic. Design each data path based on its specific consistency and latency requirements, not one global setting for the whole app.

PACELC is more useful than CAP because it captures the trade-off you make every day, not just during rare partitions. Next time someone says their system is CP or AP, ask them: 'What about when there's no partition?' That's usually where the real architecture decision lives.
